items.title: Jack DeJohnette interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, April 7, 2025
items.q: So Roscoe and Joseph Jarman and Malachi Favors, we were all sort of playing in that orchestra, and formed small groups from that orchestra.

ctx.x: Well before you left Chicago, is that when you had an interaction with the members of the AACM? Can you tell me about that?

Well it wasn’t the AACM when I was there. I left the year before the AACM was formed. But the year before that one of my mentors, Muhal Richard Abrams formed the, oh what was it – the Orchestra — Experimental Orchestra. So Roscoe and Joseph Jarman and Malachi Favors, we were all sort of playing in that orchestra, and formed small groups from that orchestra. But then I left the next year and then that’s when Roscoe Mitchell and I think Joseph Jarman, Anthony Braxton I think, yeah. That’s when it was officially…
Was their approach to music startling to you or just something —

items.title: Jack DeJohnette — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: playing with Muhal, playing with Roscoe, playing with Joseph

ctx.x: So the rhythm hadn't freed up is what I'm trying to say. This is 1960, that's when "Free Jazz" [came out], so I'm just wondering. When do the drummers begin to free up the time?

Well it happened in Chicago but it just wasn't as documented. I mean, some of the Delmark stuff. Yeah, playing with Muhal, playing with Roscoe, playing with Joseph, I was already doing that in Chicago. And Sun Ra, some of that was happening then. In New York it was more championed by Cecil Taylor and Rashied and Milford. Then those recordings: Ran Blake, Giuseppe Logan, Albert and Don Ayler.
Right, that would have been Sunny playing with them. How about Dennis Charles? Because he played with Cecil in the late 50's but I can't recall whether or not he was playing...
